title: GOFAI: Symbolic AI
subtitle: Logic, search, rules and planning: how Good Old-Fashioned AI reasons, with runnable Python labs and a search visualiser
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A hands-on course in symbolic AI, also called Good Old-Fashioned AI: its history, knowledge representation with networks and frames, propositional and predicate logic with resolution and unification, uninformed and heuristic search, game playing with minimax and alpha-beta, rule-based and expert systems, STRIPS planning and the frame problem, constraint satisfaction and Prolog, and the limits and legacy of the approach including neuro-symbolic AI. Every chapter has Python labs, and an interactive grid shows breadth-first, depth-first and A* search side by side.

chapters.title: What GOFAI is: symbols, rules and the dream of reasoning machines

maps.title: GOFAI
links: Symbol | stands for | A thing or idea
Knowledge base | stores | Facts and rules

summary: GOFAI, Good Old-Fashioned Artificial Intelligence, is the approach that builds intelligence from explicit symbols and rules: facts written down, logic applied to them, and search through possible answers. The name was coined by the philosopher John Haugeland in 1985.
It dominated AI from the 1950s to the 1980s and produced theorem provers, game players, planners and expert systems. Its rival, connectionism, learns patterns in numbers, as neural networks do.
This course teaches the core ideas with small programs you can run: representation, logic, search, rules, planning, constraints and what GOFAI could not do.

glossary.def: Good Old-Fashioned AI: intelligence built from explicit symbols and rules.
A token that stands for something, such as a fact, object or action.
A collection of facts and rules a program can reason over.
Newell and Simon's claim that a system that manipulates symbols has what is needed for general intelligence.
The approach that models intelligence with networks of simple units that learn from data.

keyPoints: GOFAI = symbols + rules + search.
Dartmouth workshop, 1956, named the field.
Logic Theorist (1956) and GPS (1957) were early programs.
Expert systems peaked in the 1980s.
AI winters followed over-promising.

items: ELI5. Some of the first thinking machines worked like a very careful child with a rulebook: write the facts down, then follow the rules to see what must be true.

When people first imagined thinking machines, they imagined machines that follow rules. A person solves a puzzle by writing down what is known and working out what follows. So a program could write facts as symbols and work out the rest by rules. That is the heart of GOFAI.
The field was named at a summer workshop at Dartmouth College in 1956, organised by John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon.
That same year Allen Newell, Herbert Simon and Cliff Shaw showed the Logic Theorist, which proved theorems from Whitehead and Russell's Principia Mathematica.

Newell and Simon followed it with the General Problem Solver in 1957, which separated what a problem is from how to search for solutions. In 1976 they stated the physical symbol system hypothesis: manipulating symbols is both necessary and sufficient for intelligent action.
Much of GOFAI is an attempt to test this claim.

In the 1970s and 1980s, expert systems captured the knowledge of human specialists as thousands of if-then rules. DENDRAL guessed chemical structures. MYCIN suggested antibiotics for blood infections. Companies invested heavily.
But the systems were brittle and costly to maintain, and funding fell in the so-called AI winters.

Today most headline AI uses learned models, but the symbolic ideas have not vanished. Search runs in route planners and game engines. Logic checks hardware and software. Knowledge graphs power web search. And recent work called neuro-symbolic AI tries to combine learning with reasoning.
Knowing GOFAI helps you see what each approach is good at.

chapters.title: Knowledge representation: networks, frames and ontologies
summary: How you write knowledge down decides what a program can do with it. A semantic network draws concepts as nodes and relations as labelled links, such as canary IS-A bird. A frame bundles slots and values for a concept, such as a bird with wings and a way of moving.
IS-A links allow inheritance: a canary inherits what is true of birds unless told otherwise. Defaults can be overridden, so a penguin IS-A bird but cannot fly.
An ontology is a shared list of categories and relations, and a knowledge graph stores facts as subject, relation, object triples.

glossary.def: A graph with concepts as nodes and labelled relations as links.
A structure of slots and values describing a typical object or situation.
A property passing from a category down to its members.
Assuming a typical property unless there is information against it.
A fact in the form subject, relation, object.

keyPoints: IS-A links build a hierarchy.
Members inherit properties from categories.
Defaults: birds fly, unless exceptions say otherwise.
Frames: slots with values and defaults.
Knowledge graph: facts as triples.

items: ELI5. A robot's brain can be a big web of words, with lines that say 'is a kind of'. Follow the lines up and you learn a canary is an animal.

Think of a family tree for ideas. Canary is a kind of bird. Bird is a kind of animal. Animal is a kind of living thing. You write each link once, and the program can answer many questions. Is a canary an animal? Follow the links up and you reach yes.

Properties move down the same links. Birds can fly, so canaries can fly. Animals breathe, so canaries breathe. You do not have to write the fact once per animal. That saving is called inheritance, and it keeps a knowledge base small and consistent.

Exceptions complicate it. Penguins are birds, but they do not fly. A good system lets a more specific fact beat a general one: the nearest node on the path wins. This is default reasoning. Dealing with the exceptions properly is one of the main reasons GOFAI got hard.

A frame gathers what is known about a type of thing. A restaurant frame has slots for menu, waiter, bill and a typical script of ordering, eating and paying. When you hear that someone went to a restaurant, the frame lets you fill in the unstated parts, which is a kind of common sense.

Modern systems store such knowledge as triples, subject, relation, object, in a knowledge graph. Wikidata and the graphs behind web search work this way. An ontology fixes the vocabulary, so different programs mean the same thing by the same word. The Semantic Web is this idea at scale.

chapters.title: Propositional logic and resolution

maps.title: Propositional logic
links: Resolution | refutes | A set of clauses
Clause | is | A disjunction of literals

summary: Propositional logic works with statements that are true or false and connectives such as not, and, or and implies. A truth table lists the value of a formula for every assignment of truth values to its variables.

A formula is a tautology if it is true in every row, satisfiable if true in some row, and a contradiction if true in none. A set of premises entails a conclusion if the conclusion is true in every row that makes all premises true.
Resolution is a single rule that is complete for refutation: to show that premises entail a goal, add the negation of the goal and derive the empty clause.

glossary.def: A formula true under every assignment.
True under at least one assignment.
A conclusion follows from premises if every assignment making the premises true makes it true.
A disjunction of literals, such as A or not B.
From (A or X) and (not A or Y) derive (X or Y).

keyPoints: n variables give 2^n rows.
Tautology: always true. Contradiction: never.
P implies Q is the same as not P or Q.
Resolution: cancel a literal and its negation.
Empty clause means contradiction.

items: ELI5. Logic is a game of true and false. If 'it rains' and 'rain means wet' are true, then 'wet' must be true too.

A statement like 'it is raining' is either true or false. Combine them with not, and, or, and implies. 'If it rains then the grass is wet' is a rule. Together with 'it rains' it lets you conclude 'the grass is wet'. This step is called modus ponens, and it is the basic move of logic.

To check a formula mechanically, build its truth table. With two variables there are four rows, with three there are eight, with n there are two to the n. That growth is why exact checking becomes slow.
The SAT problem, deciding if any row works, is hard in general, though modern solvers handle huge cases.

A formula true in every row is a tautology, such as P or not P. If a conclusion is true in every row where the premises are true, we say the premises entail it. This is semantic entailment, the thing we want programs to decide correctly.

Resolution works on clauses, which are ORs of literals. Convert each formula to clauses. Take two clauses, one with A and one with not A, and merge the rest: (A or X) and (not A or Y) give (X or Y). Repeating until the empty clause appears shows the set is inconsistent.

To prove that premises entail a goal by resolution, add the negation of the goal to the clauses and see if you can reach the empty clause. This refutation proof is complete, which means it always finds a proof when one exists.
It underlies automated theorem provers and the SAT solvers used in chip design.

chapters.title: Predicate logic and unification

maps.title: Predicate logic
links: Most general unifier | is | The simplest match

summary: Predicate logic adds objects, predicates and quantifiers to propositional logic. It lets you say all humans are mortal and Socrates is human, so Socrates is mortal.

To apply a general rule to a particular fact, a program must match patterns. Unification finds a substitution of variables that makes two terms identical, such as turning Human(x) and Human(Socrates) into the same term by setting x to Socrates.
Unification is the core operation of resolution theorem provers and of Prolog.

glossary.def: A property or relation applied to objects, such as Human(Socrates).
For all or there exists, binding a variable.
A mapping from variables to terms.
A substitution that makes two terms identical.
A test that stops a variable being bound to a term containing itself.

keyPoints: All humans are mortal: for all x, Human(x) implies Mortal(x).
Variables begin with a lowercase letter; constants are capitalised, in this course.
Unify Human(x) with Human(Socrates): x = Socrates.
A variable can unify with any term not containing itself.
Different constants never unify.

items: ELI5. When a rule says 'every person is mortal', the robot must match it to 'Socrates is a person'. Matching the pattern is called unification.

Propositional logic cannot say much about the world. You need a different proposition for every person: SocratesIsHuman, PlatoIsHuman, and so on. Predicate logic fixes this. Human is a predicate, and Human(x) is a statement about any object x.
A quantifier binds x: for all x, if x is human then x is mortal.

Now the program has a rule with a variable and a fact with a constant. To use the rule it must match them. Human(x) against Human(Socrates): the predicate is the same, and the argument x can be Socrates. The substitution, written x maps to Socrates, makes both sides identical.
This matching is unification.

Unification works recursively. Two constants unify only if they are equal. A variable unifies with any term, and the binding is recorded. Two compound terms unify if they have the same name and number of arguments and every pair of arguments unifies under one consistent substitution.
Otherwise unification fails.

A catch is the occurs check. Unifying x with F(x) would need an infinite term, so a correct unifier refuses. Prolog historically skipped this check for speed, which can lead to odd behaviour. Many modern systems offer it as an option.

Unification gives GOFAI much of its power. Resolution for predicate logic unifies a literal with a negated literal, then resolves. Prolog does the same in a fixed order, which makes logic into a programming language. Planners and parsers use it to match patterns against facts.

chapters.title: Search: finding answers by exploring
summary: Many AI problems are search problems: a start state, operators that move from one state to another, and a goal test. Finding a route, solving a puzzle or planning a move are all ways of exploring a graph of states.

Breadth-first search expands states level by level, and finds a shortest path when every step costs the same. Depth-first search goes deep along one branch first, using little memory but possibly missing short answers.
The enemy of search is the exponential growth of states with depth, called the combinatorial explosion.

glossary.def: The set of all states reachable from the start by applying operators.
The states that have been found but not yet expanded.
Search that expands the shallowest states first, using a queue.
Search that expands the deepest state first, using a stack.
The average number of operators applicable in a state.

keyPoints: BFS uses a queue; DFS uses a stack.
BFS is complete and finds fewest steps.
DFS uses less memory but is not optimal.
Branching b and depth d give about b^d states.
Keep a visited set to avoid loops.

items: ELI5. To find your way out of a maze, you can try every path by rings, or run down one path as far as it goes. Both are ways of searching.

Think of a maze as a graph. Each junction is a state, each corridor an operator that takes you to a neighbouring junction. The start is where you are, and the goal is the exit. Search is the systematic way to try the junctions without going round in circles.

Breadth-first search explores in rings. First all the junctions one step away, then two steps away, and so on. It keeps the found-but-unvisited junctions in a queue, first in first out. The first time it reaches the goal, it has used the fewest possible steps.

Depth-first search chooses one corridor and follows it as far as it goes, backing up only when stuck. It keeps junctions in a stack. It needs little memory since it stores only one path, but it can wander down a long wrong path and return a long answer when a short one exists.

The cost is the number of states. If every state has b choices and the answer is d steps away, breadth-first search may look at about b to the power d states. Chess has about thirty moves per position, so looking ahead ten moves would need on the order of 30 to the 10th power, far too many.
This is the combinatorial explosion.

To avoid loops, keep a set of visited states and never expand one twice. To avoid blind exploration, use extra knowledge to guide the search, which is the idea of heuristics in the next chapter. The widget in this chapter lets you see the difference between the strategies on a grid.

practice.title: Count states
practice.intro: Write states(b, d): the number of nodes in a complete search tree with branching factor b and depth d (the root counts as depth 0): 1 + b + b^2 + ... + b^d.
practice.hint: Add up the powers of b.
practice.solution:
def states(b, d):
    total = 0
    p = 1
    for i in range(d + 1):
        total = total + p
        p = p * b
    return total

chapters.title: Heuristic search and A*

maps.title: Heuristic search
links: A star | adds | Cost so far
Manhattan distance | is | A grid heuristic

summary: A heuristic is a rule of thumb that estimates how far a state is from the goal. Using it to choose which state to expand next makes search much faster than blind search.
A* orders states by f = g + h, where g is the cost so far and h is the heuristic estimate to go. If h never overestimates the true cost (it is admissible), A* finds a cheapest path.
On a grid the Manhattan distance, the sum of horizontal and vertical steps, is a common admissible heuristic.

glossary.def: An estimate of the remaining cost from a state to the goal.
A heuristic that never overestimates the true remaining cost.
Best-first search that expands the state with the lowest g plus h.
A queue that always returns the item with the lowest key.
The sum of the absolute differences in x and y.

keyPoints: f(n) = g(n) + h(n).
Admissible: h(n) never exceeds the true cost.
Admissible h gives optimal A*.
Greedy search uses only h and is not optimal.
Manhattan distance for 4-way grids.

items: ELI5. A good guess about how far the goal is makes search much quicker, like knowing the exit is to the north-east.

Blind search treats every direction the same. But you often have a hunch. If you want to go north-east, a path going south-west is probably wasted. A heuristic turns the hunch into a number: an estimate of how far each state is from the goal.

Greedy best-first search always expands the state that looks closest to the goal. It can be quick, but it can also be fooled. A route that heads straight at the goal may run into a wall and end up far longer than a detour. It does not weigh the cost already paid.

A* fixes this by adding the two. For each state, g is the cost from the start so far and h is the estimated cost to the goal. A* always expands the state with the smallest f, the sum. If h never overestimates, A* is both complete and optimal.

On a grid where you move up, down, left or right, the Manhattan distance, the sum of the x and y differences, never overestimates, because you must make at least that many steps. If diagonal moves are allowed, the straight-line distance or the larger of the two differences is safer.

Designing heuristics is a classic GOFAI skill. For the sliding-tile puzzle, the number of misplaced tiles and the sum of Manhattan distances of tiles are both admissible, and the second is stronger. A stronger admissible heuristic means fewer states to search.

chapters.title: Game playing: minimax and alpha-beta
summary: For two-player games with perfect information, GOFAI builds a game tree of moves and counter-moves. Minimax assumes both sides play the best they can: MAX picks the move with the highest value and MIN picks the lowest.
Real games are too big to search completely, so programs search to a depth limit and score positions with an evaluation function that counts material, mobility and similar features.
Alpha-beta pruning gives the same result as minimax while skipping branches that cannot affect the answer, which roughly doubles the reachable depth.

glossary.def: A rule that chooses the move maximising the worst-case outcome against a best-playing opponent.
A function that scores a non-final position for one side.
Minimax with cut-offs for branches that cannot change the result.
Misjudging a position because a threat lies just past the search depth.
A game in which one player's gain equals the other's loss.

keyPoints: MAX picks the largest child value; MIN the smallest.
Leaves hold scores; internal nodes get backed-up values.
Alpha-beta never changes the minimax value.
Good move ordering prunes more.
Deep Blue beat Kasparov in 1997 using search.

items: ELI5. A game player thinks ahead: 'if I do this, you do that, then I do this', and picks the move that is best even if you play your best.

Draw the possible moves as a tree. At the root it is your turn, and each branch is a move. At each child it is the opponent's turn with their own branches, and so on down to the end of the game or a chosen depth. This is the game tree.

Give each end position a score from your point of view: plus one for a win, zero for a draw, minus one for a loss. Now work upward. At a node where you move, take the highest child value. Where the opponent moves, assume they take the lowest.
The value at the root is what you can guarantee against best play. That is minimax.

Chess has too many positions to search to the end, so programs stop at a depth limit and use an evaluation function. A simple one counts the value of pieces: pawns one, knights and bishops three, rooks five, queen nine. Better ones add king safety, pawn structure and mobility.
Alpha-beta pruning tracks the best value MAX can already get (alpha) and the best MIN can already hold (beta). If a branch can no longer improve on those bounds, the rest of it is skipped.
The final answer is unchanged, but with good move ordering the program searches about twice as deep in the same time.

This approach reached its peak with IBM's Deep Blue, which beat world champion Garry Kasparov in 1997 with special chips searching hundreds of millions of positions per second. It was brute force guided by hand-built evaluation, a showpiece for GOFAI. Later programs used learning instead.

chapters.title: Rule-based systems and expert systems
summary: A production system has a set of if-then rules, a working memory of facts, and an inference engine that matches rules against facts and fires them. Expert systems apply this to specialised fields such as medicine and chemistry.
Forward chaining starts with known facts and fires rules to derive new ones until nothing changes. Backward chaining starts with a goal and works back to see which facts would prove it.
Expert systems like MYCIN also attach certainty factors and can explain their reasoning by showing the rules used.

glossary.def: A statement of the form IF conditions THEN conclusions.
The set of facts currently believed true.
Reasoning from facts to conclusions by firing rules.
Reasoning from a goal to the facts needed to support it.
A person who turns an expert's knowledge into rules.

keyPoints: IF conditions THEN conclusion.
Forward chaining is data-driven.
Backward chaining is goal-driven.
Explanation: show the rules that fired.
The knowledge acquisition bottleneck: rules are hard to collect.

items: ELI5. An expert system is a long list of if-then tips from a human expert, and a little engine that follows them.

Ask a doctor how they diagnose and you may hear rules. If the patient has a fever and a stiff neck, then suspect meningitis. An expert system writes such rules as data and lets a general engine run them. The engine does not know medicine. All the knowledge is in the rules.

In forward chaining, the engine keeps a pool of facts. It looks for rules whose conditions are all in the pool, fires one and adds its conclusion to the pool. It repeats until no new facts appear. This suits situations where data arrives and you want to see what follows.

In backward chaining the engine begins with a question. Is this bacterial infection caused by this organism? It looks for rules that conclude this, then makes their conditions into new questions. It asks the user for facts it cannot derive. Prolog works this way, and it asks only what it needs.

MYCIN, built at Stanford in the 1970s, had about six hundred rules and gave certainty factors between minus one and one. It matched the advice of specialists in tests, and could explain by listing the rules it used. It was never used in practice, partly for legal and ethical reasons.

Expert systems met limits. Collecting rules from experts was slow, called the knowledge acquisition bottleneck. Large rule sets became hard to maintain and interact in unexpected ways. The systems failed ungracefully outside their narrow domain.
Even so, the rule-based approach lives on in business rules and decision engines.

chapters.title: Planning: STRIPS and the frame problem

maps.title: Planning
links: State | is | A set of facts
Action | has | Add and delete lists
Plan | is | A sequence of actions
Frame problem | asks | What stays the same

summary: Planning finds a sequence of actions that turns an initial state into a goal state. In STRIPS, a state is a set of facts, and each action has preconditions that must hold, an add list of facts it makes true, and a delete list of facts it makes false.

Applying an action to a state removes the delete list and adds the add list, leaving everything else unchanged. Planning is then a search over states, where good heuristics and clever representations matter.
The frame problem is the difficulty of stating, in a general logic, everything that an action does not change.

glossary.def: The Stanford Research Institute Problem Solver, and the action format it introduced.
A fact that must hold before an action can be applied.
The facts an action makes true and the facts it makes false.
The problem of representing what does not change when an action occurs.
Reducing the difference between current state and goal, as in GPS.

keyPoints: State = set of facts.
Apply: new = (state minus delete) plus add.
Applicable if preconditions are a subset of state.
Plan = sequence of applicable actions reaching the goal.
STRIPS assumption solves the frame problem for simple domains.

items: ELI5. A plan is a list of steps. Each step needs some things to be true first, and changes some things. The hard part is saying what does not change.

Imagine a robot in a world of blocks. A state is a set of facts such as OnTable(A), On(B, A), Clear(B), HandEmpty. The goal might be On(A, B). An action such as Unstack(B, A) needs Clear(B), On(B, A) and HandEmpty, and changes the state.

A STRIPS action lists preconditions, an add list and a delete list. Unstack(B, A) adds Holding(B) and Clear(A), and deletes On(B, A), Clear(B) and HandEmpty. To apply it, check the preconditions are in the state, remove the deleted facts and insert the added facts. All other facts stay as they were.

A plan is a sequence of actions such that each one is applicable when its turn comes, and the final state contains the goal. A planner searches for such a sequence. Forward search starts from the initial state, and backward search starts from the goal and works out what must hold before.

That last sentence in the STRIPS definition, all other facts stay as they were, hides a deep problem. In general logic, you have to say explicitly that moving a block does not change the colour of the table, the position of the other blocks, or the weather.
Writing all those frame axioms is impractical. McCarthy and Hayes named this the frame problem in 1969.

STRIPS sidesteps it by assuming that anything not in the add or delete lists stays unchanged. That works in tidy worlds, but fails when actions have indirect effects or when the world changes by itself.
Modern planners such as those using PDDL, a descendant of STRIPS, power logistics, scheduling and robotics, with heuristics that make them fast.

chapters.title: Constraints and logic programming

maps.title: Constraints
links: Horn clause | has | One positive literal

summary: A constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) has variables, each with a domain of possible values, and constraints on combinations of values. Map colouring, scheduling and Sudoku are classic examples.

Backtracking search assigns variables one at a time and undoes a choice when a constraint is violated. Constraint propagation prunes domains early, such as removing values that conflict with a neighbour's only remaining value.
Logic programming, as in Prolog, states facts and rules as Horn clauses and answers queries by backward chaining with unification and backtracking.

glossary.def: A problem defined by variables, domains and constraints.
A depth-first search that undoes assignments that lead to a violation.
Using constraints to remove impossible values from domains.
A clause with at most one positive literal, the form used by Prolog.
A logic programming language based on Horn clauses and backward chaining.

keyPoints: CSP = variables + domains + constraints.
Backtracking: assign, check, undo.
Choose the most constrained variable first.
Prolog: facts, rules and queries.
Prolog searches depth-first with backtracking.

items: ELI5. Colouring a map so neighbours differ is a puzzle of choices and rules. Try a colour, and if you get stuck, undo and try another.

A map-colouring puzzle asks for a colour for each region so that no two neighbouring regions share a colour. Regions are the variables, the colours are the domain, and the constraint is that neighbours differ.
The same pattern fits timetabling, where classes are variables, time slots are the domain and clashes are forbidden.
The basic method is backtracking. Pick a variable, try a value, and check the constraints. If it is fine, move on to the next variable. If no value works, go back and change an earlier choice.
This is depth-first search with early failure, and it avoids exploring any branch that has already broken a constraint.

Heuristics speed it up a great deal. Choosing the variable with the fewest remaining values, the most constrained one, finds dead ends sooner. Constraint propagation, such as arc consistency, removes values that cannot be part of any solution before search even starts. Sudoku solvers work this way.
Prolog turns logic into a programming language. A program is a set of facts and rules, such as parent(tom, bob) and grandparent(X, Z) :- parent(X, Y), parent(Y, Z).
A query such as grandparent(tom, Who) is answered by backward chaining, unifying each goal with facts and rule heads, and backtracking when a choice fails.
Prolog, created by Colmerauer and Kowalski in the early 1970s, was chosen for Japan's Fifth Generation Computer project in the 1980s.

That project did not deliver the expected breakthroughs, but Prolog and constraint solvers are still used in scheduling, configuration and language processing, and its ideas live on in modern solvers.

chapters.title: Limits, legacy and the road to neuro-symbolic AI

maps.title: Legacy
links: Symbol grounding | asks | Where meaning comes from

summary: GOFAI ran into walls. Everyday common sense turned out to need millions of facts and exceptions. Rule systems were brittle at the edges of their knowledge, and the frame, qualification and ramification problems made precise logical descriptions of the world endless.

Projects like Cyc, started by Douglas Lenat in 1984, tried to write down common sense by hand, and are still running. Meanwhile, learning from data overtook hand-written rules in vision, speech and language.

The symbolic legacy remains in search, planning, verification, databases and knowledge graphs. Neuro-symbolic AI tries to give learned systems the ability to reason, and symbolic systems the ability to learn.

glossary.def: Everyday facts and expectations that people share, such as water making things wet.
A long-running project to encode common-sense knowledge in formal logic.
The question of how symbols get meaning beyond other symbols.
The tendency of rule systems to fail sharply outside their narrow domain.
Approaches that combine neural networks with symbolic reasoning.

keyPoints: Common sense needs huge amounts of knowledge.
Rule systems are brittle at their edges.
Searle's Chinese Room argued against pure symbol manipulation.
Symbolic ideas survive in search, planning and verification.
Neuro-symbolic AI mixes learning and reasoning.

items: ELI5. Old-style AI was good at clear rules but bad at everyday common sense. New AI learns from examples. Putting the two together is an exciting idea.

People know without thinking that a glass dropped on a hard floor will break, that you cannot pour a liquid into a closed bottle, and that an elephant does not fit in a car. Nobody listed these facts for us.
Writing them all down turned out to be vast, because each fact has exceptions, and each exception has exceptions.

Cyc is the boldest attempt. Beginning in 1984, a team has entered millions of assertions about the everyday world in a formal language and written inference rules over them. It is useful for some tasks.
But after forty years, it has not reached the broad understanding its founders hoped for, which many see as a sign of the limits of hand-coding.

Philosophers raised deeper doubts. John Searle's Chinese Room argued in 1980 that shuffling symbols by rules, however well done, does not give understanding. The symbol grounding problem asks how a symbol can mean anything without a link to the world.
Defenders replied that understanding may arise from the whole system, and the debate continues.

After 2010, deep learning delivered large gains on perception and language without hand-written rules. It learns from examples, copes with noise and needs no knowledge engineer. But it has its own weaknesses: errors that are hard to explain, a need for lots of data, and uncertain reasoning.
These are exactly what symbolic methods were designed for.

So the symbolic ideas are far from dead. Search guides game programs and route planners. Logic verifies chips and software. Knowledge graphs power search engines and assistants. Neuro-symbolic systems pair neural perception with a reasoning step, or let language models call a solver.
Studying GOFAI gives you the other half of the toolbox.
